“Of course he was very entertaining, and so on, but I was terribly disappointed. When I asked about the chain mail, he just laughed and said it was much too cold to wear in England. Ah, here comes Mr. Podgers! Mr. Podgers, please read the Duchess of Paisley’s palm. Duchess, take off your glove. No, the other hand, not the left.”

“Dear Gladys, I really don’t think this is quite proper,” the Duchess said, hesitantly unbuttoning a rather grubby soft leather glove.

“Nothing interesting ever is,” Lady Windermere replied. “That is how the world was made. But first, introductions. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my favorite palm reader. Mr. Podgers, the Duchess of Paisley. If you tell me her mount of the moon is larger than mine, I shall never trust you again.”

“I’m sure there is nothing like that in my hand, Gladys,” the Duchess said seriously.

“Your Grace is correct,” Mr. Podgers said, looking at the small, fat hand and its short, square fingers. “The mount of the moon is undeveloped. Your life line, however, is excellent. Please bend your wrist. Thank you. Three clear bracelet lines! You will live to a great age, Duchess, and be very happy. Ambition: extremely moderate. The intellect line: not overdeveloped. The heart line—”

“Do say something indiscreet, Mr. Podgers!” Lady Windermere cried.

“I would be delighted,” he answered with a bow, “if the Duchess had ever been indiscreet. Unfortunately, I see very lasting affection joined to a strong sense of duty.”

“Please continue,” the Duchess said, looking quite pleased.

“Thrift is certainly among Your Grace’s virtues,” Mr. Podgers continued. Lady Windermere burst out laughing.

“Thrift is a very good thing,” the Duchess remarked complacently. “When I married Paisley, he had eleven castles and not one house fit to live in.”

“And now he has twelve houses and no castles,” Lady Windermere exclaimed.

“Well, my dear,” said the Duchess, “I like—”

“Comfort,” Mr. Podgers supplied. “Modern conveniences and hot water in every bedroom. Your Grace is quite right. Comfort is the only gift our civilization can offer.”

“You have described the Duchess’s character wonderfully. Now you must read Lady Flora’s.” At a nod from the smiling hostess, a tall girl with sandy Scottish hair and high shoulder blades stepped awkwardly from behind the sofa. She offered a long, bony hand with fingers that widened at the tips.

“Ah, a pianist,” Mr. Podgers said. “An excellent pianist, though perhaps hardly a musician.

When I returned, this letter from my father awaited me:

“My dear Victor,

“You have doubtless been impatient for a letter appointing the day of your return. At first I considered writing only a few words to say when I would expect you. But such kindness would be cruel, and I dare not do it. Imagine your astonishment, my son, if, looking for a joyful welcome, you encountered only tears and misery! Yet how, Victor, am I to tell you of our calamity? Long absence cannot have made you indifferent to our happiness and sorrow; how can I cause pain to my son, so long away? I would prepare you for this grievous news, but know it cannot be done. Already your eyes must be hastening over the page in search of the words that announce the dreadful event.

“William is dead! That gentle, merry child, whose smiles cheered and warmed my heart! Victor, he has been murdered!

“I shall offer no attempt at comfort, but simply describe what occurred.

“Last Thursday, May 7th, my niece, your two brothers, and I walked in Plainpalais. The evening was peaceful and warm, and we continued farther than our custom. Dusk had fallen before we thought of going home. Then we found that William and Ernest, who had run ahead, were nowhere to be seen. We sat upon a bench to await them. Soon Ernest appeared and asked whether we had seen his brother. They had been playing together, he said, when William ran off to hide. Ernest had searched unsuccessfully and then waited a long while, but William had not returned.

“His story disturbed us, and we searched until night came. Elizabeth then suggested that William might have gone home. He was not there. We went out again with torches, for I could not rest while imagining my dear boy lost and exposed to the damp and dew of night. Elizabeth, too, was in terrible distress. At about five in the morning I found my beautiful child, whom only the previous evening I had seen lively and blooming with health, lying discoloured and still upon the grass. The murderer’s finger had left its mark on his neck.

“He was carried home, and the suffering written on my face revealed the truth to Elizabeth. She urgently begged to see his body. I first tried to dissuade her, but she insisted. Entering the room where he lay, she quickly examined the victim’s throat, clasped her hands, and cried, ‘O God!

They were bringing along a very respectable-looking older gentleman and a pleasant-looking younger man with his right arm in a sling. Good heavens, how everyone shouted and laughed, on and on! I couldn’t see anything funny, and I figured the duke and king would have a hard time finding the joke too. I expected them to go pale. But they didn’t lose a trace of color. The duke gave no sign that he suspected what was happening. He went happily gurgling about, satisfied as a jug pouring out buttermilk. The king kept gazing sorrowfully at the newcomers, as though the thought that such frauds and villains existed gave his very heart a stomachache. He played it beautifully. Plenty of the leading townspeople gathered around him to show their support. The newly arrived old gentleman looked utterly bewildered. Before long he began speaking, and I could tell at once that he sounded English—different from the king, though the king’s imitation was pretty good. I can’t reproduce the old man’s words or copy his accent, but he turned to the crowd and said something like this:

“This is an unexpected surprise, and I freely admit that I am poorly prepared to answer it. My brother and I have suffered some misfortunes. He has broken his arm, and our luggage was mistakenly put ashore at a town upriver during the night. I am Harvey, Peter Wilks’s brother, and this is our brother William. He can neither hear nor speak, and with only one hand available he can barely communicate in signs either. We are exactly who we say we are. In a day or two, once I recover our luggage, I can prove it. Until then, I’ll say no more. We will go to the hotel and wait.”

He and the other man started away. The king laughed and blurted out:

“Broken his arm! Very likely, isn’t it? And very convenient for a fraud who needs to use signs but hasn’t learned any. Lost their luggage! That’s excellent—and wonderfully clever, under the circumstances!”

He laughed again, and everyone joined in except three or four people, perhaps half a dozen. One was the doctor. Another was a sharp-looking gentleman who had just left the steamboat, carrying an old-fashioned bag made of carpet. He was speaking quietly to the doctor, and they kept glancing toward the king and nodding. This was Levi Bell, the lawyer who had gone to Louisville. Another was a big, rough, powerful fellow who had come up, heard everything the old gentleman said, and was now listening to the king.
